title: Ancient Trees in the United Kingdom: Cities to Explore
meta_description: Britain's oldest trees are yews, and churches kept most of them alive. London's Totteridge Yew is put at two thousand years. Eight cities, 68 trees.
intro: Britain's oldest trees are yews, and it is churches, not palaces, that kept most of them standing. London's Totteridge Yew is put at two thousand years old, roughly a millennium and a half older than the church built beside it, one of many British yews reckoned to predate Christianity in these islands. Oaks tell a different story: a mild, fire-free climate let them stand long enough to earn names tied to real dates, a Domesday Oak already growing when the Conquest was surveyed in 1086, a Royal Oak enclosed inside a park wall in 1637 because it was already centuries old. Age here survives less through law than inheritance, a landed estate, a cathedral close, a royal park that changed hands but never changed use. Eight cities are mapped so far, from Edinburgh's botanic garden to Oxford's college quadrangles, and wherever a yew appears it tends to win on age.
